clue.text: One in film crowd unsettled without Bond, New Zealand one — some show!

parts.note: an extra is a background player in a crowd scene

taken as written, the part to be removed
NZ is the abbreviation for New Zealand
a means one

explanation.surface: A film extra joins a restless crowd scene missing James Bond, plus a New Zealander, in quite a production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' looks like 007 but is just the letters taken off the end of the wanderer word.
explanation.definitionFit: An extravaganza is a lavish, spectacular entertainment, so the exclamation 'some show!' captures it.

clue.text: Country worried about act being modified, showing procrastination

the letters of act, rearranged

explanation.surface: A nation fretting while some act is being amended sounds like a government dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are scrambled: the larger mix opens to hold the smaller after its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cunctatory means delaying, from Latin cunctator, a delayer, the nickname of Fabius who stalled Hannibal.

clue.text: Light sailing-ship from Sri Lanka with a party on board

taken as written
a rave is a lively party

clue.text: Wife admits rising naughtiness with Evelyn initially, i.e. non gender specific?

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the wife word takes the rest inside it

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the name before it

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A wife puts up with growing mischief involving Evelyn, a name that suits either sex.
explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn is a name given to both men and women, which is why the surface ends with 'i.e.' and a gender question.
explanation.definitionFit: Unisex describes clothing, styles or names designed to suit both sexes alike.

clue.text: Almost give away? Ha'pence is silly

indicators.note: something silly is muddled and foolish, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the halfpennies word, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Offering halfpennies would be nearly giving something away, which is daft.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha'pence was an old British halfpenny coin. To make something cheaper is to bring it close to giving it away.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheapen goods is to lower their price, which taken far enough comes near to handing them over for free.

clue.text: Tottie unusually bags particular product in waistcoat material

explanation.surface: A woman called Tottie, out of character, picks up a particular item made of waistcoat fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilinette is a fabric of silk or cotton with woollen weft, once used chiefly for waistcoats.

clue.text: Pain in extremity, short time bandaged

clue.text: R. Blanc's art goes into exotic bread and potato dish

clue.text: Give catch?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: give way, submit or bend under pressure
second meaning: the amount produced or caught, a harvest

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it look like a single request to hand over a catch; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to give way; as a noun it means the produce or haul gathered from a crop or fishery.

clue.text: The end of life (12, three words)

parts.note: surface reading: the moment a life finishes
setter's reading: the end as a boundary or portal through which one passes out of life, a biblical image

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is biblical (Job 38:17, 'Have the gates of death been opened unto thee?'), picturing dying as passing through a portal.
explanation.definitionFit: The entrance to death is pictured as a gateway at the border of life, so it stands for life's ending.

clue.text: Cross worker, this, hair in a tangle about nothing, giving jaundiced look?

the letters of hair, rearranged and opened up

clue.text: A bit of advanced maths, old stuff

definitions.meaning: first meaning: short for trigonometry, a branch of mathematics
second meaning: an archaic verb meaning to fill or stuff full

clue.text: Street with posh hotel, international one containing wing for showy plant genus

explanation.walkthrough: The wing goes into the hotel after its first letter, not around the whole string.

clue.text: Old soak, in avoiding wine etc, missing clubs

indicators.note: avoiding means keeping away from, so these two letters are left out of the phrase
missing means lacking, so the card-suit letter is dropped as well

parts.note: the phrase taken as written, spaces ignored

taken as written, letters to be removed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old soak' looks like a drunkard, but it is a verb, an archaic word meaning to wet.
explanation.definitionFit: Weet is an old and Scots form of wet, so it can mean to soak or drench.

clue.text: Rogue sailor on junk possibly mixing up his port and starboard?

explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a scoundrel or mischievous rogue.

clue.text: Untidy mass to observe (old-style), Latin included

clue.text: Oxford dreamers heading for renown in M16?

indicators.note: 'in' puts the selected letter inside the intelligence word

parts.note: MI6 is Britain's foreign intelligence service, staffed by spies; the clue prints the digit 1 for the letter I

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Oxford dreamers head off for fame in the secret service, like the Cambridge spies.
explanation.walkthrough: Matthew Arnold called Oxford 'that sweet city with her dreaming spires', so its spires are the dreamers. MI6 is the UK Secret Intelligence Service.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford's skyline of towers is famously described as dreaming spires, making the steeples themselves its dreamers.

clue.text: No longer disturbed old soldier with cross engraved?

X is the shape of a cross

explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' marks the answer as obsolete, not as the absence of disturbance: the old spelling of vexed.
explanation.definitionFit: Vext is an archaic spelling of vexed, meaning annoyed or troubled.

clue.text: Huge –'s whizzing? 'See me go with huskies!'

definitions.text: Huge –'s whizzing? 'See me go with huskies!'

indicators.note: whizzing means rushing about at speed, so the letters are flung into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, letters to be set aside
taken as written, a letter to be set aside

explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the dash stands for the answer, and 'Huge' plus the answer plus 's', jumbled, make 'me go huskies'. So take those extra letters out of that phrase and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit traveller is the figure traditionally pictured driving a husky sled across the snow.

clue.text: Celebrating early printer, date's given in a piece of type?
